messages.author: c6823c7fe297889f
messages.subject: incorporating variability in model predictors
parts:
Hopefully this question has not been addressed already, but I have not been able to find an answer. I am having trouble writing a stan code that can incorporate variability in a model predictor. The model itself is a fairly straightforward multiple regression with random effects, but one of the predictor variables are estimates with associated variance. So, for predictor x (a vector. length N) I have a second vector, s (length N), with a unique variance for each value of x. I am trying to write code that will redefine a new vector, x_new, at each iteration of the MCMC run by sampling from the distributions defined by x and s, ie: x_new~normal(x,s). In all of my attempts the posterior mean values of x_new drift away from their intended values, x. This makes sense, because I have had to define x_new in the transformed parameter or model blocks. Stan therefore treats x_new as a parameter with an informative prior. But, what I want is for x_new to be treated as data that varies at each iteration, not as parameters to be estimated.

I am fairly sure this should be possible, but maybe not without a random sampler in the transformed parameters block? Can this be done with stan?. 

-Devin

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] incorporating variability in model predictors
parts:
Devin,
You have to do a measurement-error model, i.e. a simultaneous equations model. I have not followed your details, but sometimes these models look like this:

y[i] ~ N (a + b*x[i], sigma_y);
x_obs[i] ~ N (x[i], sigma_x);

And you need an informative prior on sigma_x. In this case, the data are y and x_obs, and x is an unknown parameter vector. I don't think this is exactly your model but the basic idea is that you need a separate line in your model for each observation.

Andrew

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] incorporating variability in model predictors
parts:
What Andrew said. Switching back to Devin's variable names
and writing out in Stan, you need:

data {
int<lower=0> N; // number of cases
vector[N] x; // measurment with error
vector<lower=0>[N]; // measurement deviation
vector[N] y; // observed outcomes
...
parameters {
vector[N] x_new; // measurement plus noise
}
model {
x_new ~ normal(x,s);

for (n in 1:N)
y[n] ~ ... x_new[n] ... // use measurement plus noise
}

The "x_new ~ normal(x,s)" is vectorized, and just
a more compact and efficient version of writing:

for (n in 1:N)
x_new[n] ~ normal(x[n],s[n]);

Hopefully the sampling for y[n] can be vectorized, too.

Instead of sampling x_new directly, you can explicitly sample
the measurement noise for each point n:

epsilon ~ normal(0,s);
x_new <- x + epsilon;

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] incorporating variability in model predictors
parts:
On 1/20/13 9:04 PM, Devin Leopold wrote:
> Andrew & Bob - thanks for your quick replies! As far as I can tell I have been doing exactly what you suggested. So at
> least I am not too far off the mark here... But still, after the model converges the distributions of the x_new values
> have diverged from the error distributions that I specified. I would expect the posterior mean of x_new to be very close
> to x_obs after 1000+ iterations, but they diverge, suggesting that they are being fitted to the model (the opposite of
> what I am trying to do by incorporating predictor error!).

Right -- the x_new[n] values are intended be fitted with
the model. The typical Bayesian approach treats them as missing
data. Specifically x_new[n] represents the true value for
case n that was measured as x[n] with noise sigmax[n].

For instance, see:

Richardson and Gilks, 1993. A Bayesian approach to measurement error...
http://www.med.mcgill.ca/epidemiology/joseph/courses/epib-675/richardson.pdf

So you have something like:

x[n] ~ normal(x_new[n],sigmax[n])

giving you the probablity of observation x[n] given true
value x_new[n] and measurement deviation sigmax[n].

Sometimes you can integrate out the effect analytically.

> x_obs~normal(x_new,sigmax) //I have tried with and without this line of code.
> x_new~normal(x_obs,sigmax)

You only want one of these.

If you have both, what you get in Stan is the
following two lines of code generated in C++,
where lp__ is the total log probability accumulator:

lp__ += normal_log(x_obs,x_new,sigmax);
lp__ += normal_log(x_new,x_obs,sigmax);

Because the variate and location parameter are interchangeable
for a normal, this is double-adding the same term to the log
probability. The usual formulation is opposite of the way
I suggested, which is to use:

x_obs ~ normal(x_new,sigmax);

That is, model distribution of the measured values x_obs
given the true values x_new and measurement errors sigmax.

Sometimes you also see a model of x_new as well, especially
if you have some other predictors to use for it.

- Bob

messages.subject: The fake-data test is always a good idea.
parts:
Devin
No, we don't have anything like the cut function.  If you have a problem where the parameter estimates don't make sense, this implies that you have additional prior information you're not using in your model, or that your model is not fitting the data.  If I were you, I'd start by fitting fake data from your model to make sure that the fitting is doing what you think it should be doing.  If it works with fake data but not with real data, I think you should alter/expand your model so that it fits your data better, rather than trying to escape the problem using a kluge!
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: incorporating variability in model predictors
parts:
No, there's nothing like a cut function in Stan or even a way
to hack it. That's intentional for reasons outlined in
Andrew's response Also, a cut function like BUGS wouldn't really
make sense in Stan because Stan's not based on nodes in
a directed acyclic graphical model.

We are going to provide forward sampling in the generated
quantities block, but this won't feed back into the model
the way you probably want.

- Bob
